claim: Mitochondrial ClpX (mtClpX) activates the initiating enzyme for heme biosynthesis, 5-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS), by promoting cofactor incorporation.
source: We previously discovered that the mitochondrial AAA+ protein unfoldase ClpX (mtClpX) activates the initiating enzyme for heme biosynthesis, 5-aminolevulinic acid synthase (ALAS), by promoting cofactor incorporation.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work by the authors (Kardon et al., 2015).

claim: mtClpX activation of ALAS is non-proteolytic but requires ATP hydrolysis and intact pore loops.
source: This activation is non-proteolytic, but requires ATP hydrolysis and intact pore loops, implicating the unfoldase activity of mtClpX in this unconventional function.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work (Kardon et al., 2015).

claim: mtClpX binds six discrete peptide sequences within ALAS.
source: mtClpX bound six discrete peptide sequences within ALAS (Figure 1A, boxed in blue; control blot showing specificity in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data from peptide array binding assays shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Five of the six mtClpX-binding sequences map to a structurally contiguous site in ALAS consisting of α-helix α1 and a region in direct hydrogen-bonding contact with α1 across the ALAS dimer interface.
source: Five of these sequences map to a structurally contiguous site in ALAS, consisting of an α-helix (α1) that is the most N-terminal structured element of ALAS, and a small region that is in direct hydrogen-bonding contact with α1 across the ALAS dimer interface (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by mapping of peptide array data onto the ALAS crystal structure shown in Figure 1B.

claim: The sixth mtClpX-binding peptide maps to a site about 40 Å from the clustered sites.
source: The sixth, most C-terminal peptide maps to a separate site about 40 Å from the clustered sites.
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis of the peptide binding sites.

claim: N-terminal fusion of DHFR with ALAS (DHFR-ALAS) blocked stimulation of PLP binding by mtClpX.
source: N-terminal fusion of DHFR with ALAS (DHFR-ALAS) blocked stimulation of PLP binding by mtClpX, but appending the N-terminal sequence of ALAS through α1 to DHFR-ALAS (α1-DHFR-ALAS) restored the ability of mtClpX to stimulate PLP binding (Figure 1D, dark blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D measuring PLP binding rates.

claim: Appending the N-terminal sequence of ALAS through α1 to DHFR-ALAS (α1-DHFR-ALAS) restored the ability of mtClpX to stimulate PLP binding.
source: N-terminal fusion of DHFR with ALAS (DHFR-ALAS) blocked stimulation of PLP binding by mtClpX, but appending the N-terminal sequence of ALAS through α1 to DHFR-ALAS (α1-DHFR-ALAS) restored the ability of mtClpX to stimulate PLP binding (Figure 1D, dark blue bars).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: Addition of methotrexate to α1-DHFR-ALAS blocked its activation by mtClpX.
source: Addition of methotrexate to α1-DHFR-ALAS blocked its activation by mtClpX (Figure 1D, dark orange bars) indicating that mtClpX acting from near the N-terminus is required for ALAS activation.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1D.

claim: mtClpX acting from near the N-terminus is required for ALAS activation.
source: Addition of methotrexate to α1-DHFR-ALAS blocked its activation by mtClpX (Figure 1D, dark orange bars) indicating that mtClpX acting from near the N-terminus is required for ALAS activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the methotrexate blocking experiment.

claim: mtClpX requires the α1 site to recognize ALAS.
source: These data support the conclusions that mtClpX requires the α1 site to recognize ALAS and acts from this site to accelerate PLP binding.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the DHFR fusion and methotrexate blocking experiments.

claim: E. coli ClpX does not act on wildtype ALAS.
source: E. coli ClpX does not act on wildtype ALAS (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: E. coli ClpX accelerated PLP binding to λO2-12-ALAS fusion protein.
source: E. coli ClpX accelerated PLP binding to this fusion protein, albeit with a slower Vmax than observed with the native mtClpX-ALAS interaction (Figure 1E, Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1E and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: An unfoldase acting from the N-terminal site is sufficient to stimulate ALAS activation.
source: Therefore, an unfoldase acting from this N-terminal site is sufficient to stimulate ALAS activation.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the E. coli ClpX experiment with λO2-12-ALAS.

claim: mtClpX processed λO2-12-ALAS more rapidly than wildtype ALAS.
source: mtClpX processed λO2-12-ALAS more rapidly than wildtype ALAS by (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1F.

claim: The mature N-terminus of ALAS corresponds to cleavage after residue 34 of the preprotein (∆34-ALAS).
source: The N-terminal sequence of this species corresponded to cleavage after residue 34 of the preprotein (∆34-ALAS), indicating that an additional 23 amino acids beyond the previously detected species (∆57-ALAS) are retained in the mature protein (Figure 2A, Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by Edman degradation data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: mtClpX activated ∆34-ALAS more rapidly than λO2-12-ALAS.
source: We tested the effect of this natural N-terminal extension of ALAS on mtClpX action and found that mtClpX activated ∆34-ALAS even more rapidly than λO2-12-ALAS (Figure 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2B.

claim: Extension of the N-terminus of ALAS principally stimulated the maximal rate of activation (nearly twenty-fold increase in Vmax by extension with the natural sequence) and modestly decreased the KM.
source: Extension of the N-terminus of ALAS, either with its natural sequence (34-57) or with λO2-12, principally stimulated the maximal rate of activation (a nearly twenty-fold increase in Vmax by extension with the natural sequence) and modestly decreased the KM (Figure 2B–D).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis data shown in Figure 2B-D.

claim: Extension of the N-terminus of ALAS reduced coprecipitation of ALAS with mtClpX.
source: Extension of the N-terminus of ALAS also reduced coprecipitation of ALAS with mtClpX (∆34-ALAS compared to ∆57-ALAS, Figure 3B), suggesting that this extension may present mild steric hindrance to static binding, although it increases the overall efficiency of mtClpX activation of ALAS and may disfavor dissociation after mtClpX actively engages ALAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: The N-terminus of Δ34-ALAS to the beginning of α1 (residue 71) exhibited near-instantaneous completion of deuterium uptake in hydrogen-deuterium exchange experiments.
source: This natural N-terminal extension of ALAS has a dynamic or disordered structure; the N-terminus of Δ34-ALAS to the beginning of α1 (residue 71) exhibited near-instantaneous completion of deuterium uptake in hydrogen-deuterium exchange experiments (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C; discussed further below).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Alanine substitution at positions F71A, Y73A, and F71A/Y73A in α1 reduced coprecipitation with mtClpX.
source: Alanine substitution at positions in α1 (F71A, Y73A, and the double substitution F71A/Y73A, Figure 3A) reduced coprecipitation with mtClpX (Figure 3B), and increased the KM for activation by mtClpX (Figure 3C–E), consistent with α1 functioning as a sequence-specific tag that recruits mtClpX to begin exerting force on ALAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by coimmunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Alanine substitution at positions F71A, Y73A, and F71A/Y73A in α1 increased the KM for activation by mtClpX.
source: Alanine substitution at positions in α1 (F71A, Y73A, and the double substitution F71A/Y73A, Figure 3A) reduced coprecipitation with mtClpX (Figure 3B), and increased the KM for activation by mtClpX (Figure 3C–E), consistent with α1 functioning as a sequence-specific tag that recruits mtClpX to begin exerting force on ALAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 3C-E.

claim: α1 functions as a sequence-specific tag that recruits mtClpX to begin exerting force on ALAS.
source: Alanine substitution at positions in α1 (F71A, Y73A, and the double substitution F71A/Y73A, Figure 3A) reduced coprecipitation with mtClpX (Figure 3B), and increased the KM for activation by mtClpX (Figure 3C–E), consistent with α1 functioning as a sequence-specific tag that recruits mtClpX to begin exerting force on ALAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the mutagenesis and binding/kinetic data.

claim: The double substitution variant (ALASF71A/Y73A) exhibited an increased rate of spontaneous PLP binding.
source: The double substitution variant (ALASF71A/Y73A) exhibited an increased rate of spontaneous PLP binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and an increased Vmax for mtClpX-stimulated PLP binding (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A.

claim: The double substitution variant (ALASF71A/Y73A) exhibited an increased Vmax for mtClpX-stimulated PLP binding.
source: The double substitution variant (ALASF71A/Y73A) exhibited an increased rate of spontaneous PLP binding (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A) and an increased Vmax for mtClpX-stimulated PLP binding (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: Y73 directly contacts the other protomer through hydrogen bonding.
source: These residues are positioned at the dimer interface: Y73 directly contacts the other protomer through hydrogen bonding, and F71A is positioned for a CH-pi interaction with P246 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: F71 is positioned for a CH-pi interaction with P246.
source: These residues are positioned at the dimer interface: Y73 directly contacts the other protomer through hydrogen bonding, and F71A is positioned for a CH-pi interaction with P246 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This claim is supported by structural analysis shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B.

claim: ALASF71A/Y73A retained only ~10–20% of wildtype activity.
source: Although F71A and Y73A single variants retained synthase activity similar to wildtype, the double variant ALASF71A/Y73A retained only ~10–20% of wildtype activity (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by enzyme activity assay data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2C.

claim: The Y274A mutation did not perturb the KM for mtClpX activation of ALAS.
source: In contrast to mutations in α1, a mutation at the surface of the mtClpX-interacting sequence cluster across the dimer interface from this helix, Y274A, did not perturb the KM for mtClpX activation of ALAS (although it did reduce coprecipitation [Figure 3B]).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: The Y274A mutation reduced the Vmax of mtClpX activation.
source: Instead, the Y274A mutation reduced the Vmax of mtClpX activation (Figure 3D,E).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic data shown in Figure 3D,E.

claim: F71A reduced and Y73A abolished mtClpX enhancement of ALA levels in vivo.
source: Within α1, F71A reduced and Y73A abolished mtClpX enhancement of ALA levels in vivo (Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo ALA measurement data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Mutation of hem1Y274A modestly reduced mtClpX-dependent ALA levels in vivo.
source: Mutation of the trans-protomer contact for mtClpX (hem1Y274A) modestly reduced mtClpX-dependent ALA levels in vivo.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo ALA measurement data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Combined mutation of hem1F71A/Y274A abolished mtClpX enhancement of ALA levels.
source: Combined mutation of this contact and of one mtClpX α1 contact (hem1F71A/Y274A) abolished mtClpX enhancement of ALA levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by in vivo ALA measurement data shown in Figure 3F.

claim: Most of ALAS exhibited either no measurable deuteration or gradual deuteration over the 60 min observation period in the absence of mtClpX.
source: ALAS conformation overall was very stable in the absence of mtClpX. Most of ALAS exhibited either no measurable deuteration or gradual deuteration over the 60 min observation period, characteristic of a tightly folded protein (with the exception of fast, immediately saturated exchange at the extreme N- and C-termini) (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: In the presence of mtClpX, deuteration was increased in defined, localized regions of ALAS over time.
source: In the presence of mtClpX, deuteration was increased in defined, localized regions of ALAS over time (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1), strongly supporting the conclusion that mtClpX enacts limited, specific conformational change(s) rather than globally unfolding ALAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 4 and Supplementary file 1.

claim: mtClpX enacts limited, specific conformational change(s) rather than globally unfolding ALAS.
source: In the presence of mtClpX, deuteration was increased in defined, localized regions of ALAS over time (Figure 4; Supplementary file 1), strongly supporting the conclusion that mtClpX enacts limited, specific conformational change(s) rather than globally unfolding ALAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the hydrogen-deuterium exchange data showing localized rather than global changes.

claim: mtClpX-induced deuterium uptake was localized to α1, the β sheet that connects α1 to the active site (β1–3) and the following active-site loop and α2, and several non-contiguous peptides surrounding the active site of ALAS.
source: mtClpX-induced deuterium uptake was localized to α1, the β sheet that connects α1 to the active site (β1–3) and the following active-site loop and α2, and several non-contiguous peptides surrounding the active site of ALAS (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 4.

claim: The mass spectra of most peptides showing mtClpX-induced deuteration existed in two populations, corresponding to the undeuterated and the maximally deuterated form, with a single transition between these forms (EX1 kinetics).
source: The mass spectra of most of these peptides existed in two populations, corresponding to the undeuterated and the maximally deuterated form, with a single transition between these forms (EX1 kinetics) (Weis et al., 2006; Figure 4A, right panel, indicated with the half-life of the EX1 unfolding event, t1/2; half-life mapped on ALAS structure in Figure 4C, lower panel), consistent with cooperative unfolding within the peptide.
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange mass spectrometry data shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: The increased exposure of ALAS by mtClpX was ATP-dependent.
source: This increased exposure was ATP-dependent and thus the result of active unfolding by mtClpX (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B and Supplementary file 1.

claim: mtClpX induced a nearly identical deuterium uptake profile in a holoenzyme preparation of ALAS as in PLP-depleted ALAS.
source: To test whether exchange in this region was the direct result of mtClpX remodeling or due to loss of PLP or PLP-oxime, we tested the effect of mtClpX on deuterium uptake of a holoenzyme preparation of ALAS as well, and observed a nearly identical uptake profile (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Inclusion of PLP in the exchange reaction only slightly suppressed some mtClpX-induced hydrogen exchange, immediately adjacent to bound PLP.
source: Inclusion of PLP in the exchange reaction only slightly suppressed some mtClpX-induced hydrogen exchange, immediately adjacent to bound PLP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E; see Supplementary file 1 for data from longer peptides with clear PLP-dependent protection), indicating that remodeling by mtClpX, rather than loss of ligand, induced nearly all of the increased exposure at each element in ALAS.
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E and Supplementary file 1.

claim: Remodeling by mtClpX, rather than loss of ligand, induced nearly all of the increased exposure at each element in ALAS.
source: Inclusion of PLP in the exchange reaction only slightly suppressed some mtClpX-induced hydrogen exchange, immediately adjacent to bound PLP (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D,E; see Supplementary file 1 for data from longer peptides with clear PLP-dependent protection), indicating that remodeling by mtClpX, rather than loss of ligand, induced nearly all of the increased exposure at each element in ALAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PLP addition experiment showing minimal effect on deuterium exchange.

claim: The EX1 unfolding half-life (t1/2) for mtClpX-induced exchange in α1 and β1–3 is shorter than the exchange further along the path (as-α2) and in the non-contiguous peptides surrounding the active site.
source: First, the EX1 unfolding half-life (t1/2) (Engen et al., 2008) for mtClpX-induced exchange in these elements is not uniform: exchange in α1 and β1–3 has a shorter t1/2 than the exchange further along this path (as-α2 indicated in Figure 1A,C) and in the non-contiguous peptides surrounding the active site (Figure 4A, right panel; Figure 4B, lower panel).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange kinetic data shown in Figure 4A and 4C.

claim: A short sequence (82–89) spanning the junction between α1 and β1 exhibited no mtClpX-induced exchange.
source: Second, a short sequence (82–89) spanning the junction between α1 and β1, elements that both exhibit fast mtClpX-induced exchange, exhibited no mtClpX-induced exchange (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by hydrogen-deuterium exchange data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The sequence 82-89 may be in contact with mtClpX when it stops translocating, suppressing deuterium exchange.
source: A possible explanation for this observation is that this sequence in contact with mtClpX when it stops translocating, suppressing deuterium exchange even as regions further into the protein are deprotected by conformational change propagating from the putative mtClpX arrest site.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observed pattern of deuterium exchange.

claim: E. coli ClpXP could degrade λO2-12-ALAS.
source: Unlike mammalian ClpXP in vitro (Kardon et al., 2015), E. coli ClpXP could degrade ALAS if provided with an E. coli-specific recognition site (λO2-12-ALAS)) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is supported by degradation assay data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Degradation of λO2-12-ALAS by E. coli ClpXP was slowed ~4 fold when ATP was reduced to concentrations that marginally supported ATPase activity (30 μM;~20% of maximal ATPase rate).
source: This degradation was slowed ~4 fold when ATP was reduced to concentrations that marginally supported ATPase activity (30 μM;~20% of maximal ATPase rate) (Figure 5B,C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by degradation kinetics data shown in Figure 5B,C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1.

claim: The rate at which E. coli ClpX stimulated PLP binding to ALAS was only two-fold reduced when the ATP concentration was reduced from saturating to minimal.
source: In contrast, the rate at which E. coli ClpX stimulated PLP binding to ALAS was only two-fold reduced when the ATP concentration was reduced from saturating to minimal (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLP binding kinetics data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: No truncations of ALAS appeared during degradation by E. coli ClpXP, even at low ATP concentrations.
source: No truncations of ALAS appeared during degradation, even at the low ATP concentrations that shift E. coli ClpX toward arrest/activation, indicating that each time E. coli ClpX engages ALAS, it either activates ALAS without translocating far enough into ALAS for the polypeptide to reach the active site of ClpP, or it bypasses the arrest site, continuing to complete unfolding and degradation.
evidence: This claim is supported by the absence of truncation products in the degradation assay gels.

claim: The arrest site in ALAS is near the beginning of the β1 strand (~40 amino acids from the N-terminus of λO2-12-ALAS).
source: These data provide an upper-limit estimate of the arrest site in ALAS near the beginning of the β1 strand (~40 amino acids from the N-terminus of λO2-12-ALAS).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the degradation data and the known distance from ClpX pore entrance to ClpP active site.

claim: The total rate of ClpX action on ALAS (activation and degradation combined) by E. coli ClpX is an order of magnitude lower than that for the native mtClpX-ALAS pair.
source: Furthermore, these data demonstrate that although appending a simple N-terminal recognition sequence to ALAS is minimally sufficient to confer partial unfolding/activation by a naïve unfoldase (here, E. coli ClpX) the total rate of ClpX action on ALAS (activation and degradation combined) is an order of magnitude lower than that for the native mtClpX-ALAS pair.
evidence: This claim is inferred from comparison of kinetic data for E. coli ClpX and mtClpX action on ALAS.

claim: Both high fidelity and efficiency in partial unfolding requires specific features of the cognate unfoldase and its interaction with the substrate.
source: Therefore, both high fidelity and efficiency in partial unfolding requires specific features of the cognate unfoldase and its interaction with the substrate.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the comparison of E. coli ClpX and mtClpX action on ALAS.

claim: mtClpX most likely stalls near the α1-β2 junction in ALAS.
source: Data from our HX MS experiments and ectopically-targeted ALAS processing by E. coli ClpX converge to indicate that mtClpX most likely stalls near the α1-β2 junction in ALAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined hydrogen-deuterium exchange and E. coli ClpX degradation data.

claim: Oxidized ALAS68x243 and ALAS88x427 both migrated as apparent monomers by SDS-PAGE when reduced, but upon oxidation exhibited a near-complete shift in mobility.
source: ALAS68x243 and ALAS88x427 both migrated as apparent monomers by SDS-PAGE when reduced, but upon oxidation exhibited a near-complete shift in mobility.
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Oxidized ALAS68x243 shifted to an apparent higher molecular weight, approximately twice that of an ALAS monomer, consistent with a cross-protomer disulfide bond.
source: Oxidized ALAS68x243 shifted to an apparent higher molecular weight, approximately twice that of an ALAS monomer, consistent with a cross-protomer disulfide bond.
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Oxidized ALAS88x427 shifted to a slightly faster-migrating species, consistent with the intramolecular crosslink between these residues.
source: Oxidized ALAS88x427 shifted to a slightly faster-migrating species, consistent with the intramolecular crosslink between these residues (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by SDS-PAGE data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: mtClpX action upon both oxidized ALAS68x243 and ALAS88x427 variants was strongly attenuated compared to wildtype ALAS.
source: mtClpX action upon both oxidized variants was strongly attenuated compared to wildtype ALAS (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLP binding assay data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: Upon reduction of the crosslink, mtClpX induced both cysteine-pair variants of ALAS to bind PLP at a similar rate as for the wildtype protein.
source: Upon reduction of the crosslink, mtClpX induced both cysteine-pair variants of ALAS to bind PLP at a similar rate as for the wildtype protein, indicating that loss of mtClpX action on these variants was specifically perturbed by disulfide bond formation (Figure 6C,D).
evidence: This claim is supported by PLP binding assay data shown in Figure 6C,D.

claim: mtClpX must unfold from the N-terminal engagement site on ALAS, extracting at least the first β strand, to activate ALAS.
source: Therefore, we conclude that mtClpX must unfold from the N-terminal engagement site on ALAS, extracting at least the first β strand, to activate ALAS (Figure 6—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is inferred from the disulfide crosslinking experiments.

claim: AAA+ protein unfoldases use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to pull apart the structures of their substrate proteins.
source: AAA+ protein unfoldases use the energy of ATP hydrolysis to pull apart the structures of their substrate proteins.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about AAA+ unfoldases.

claim: AAA+ unfoldases grip the substrate polypeptide with aromatic side chains of pore-1 loops that protrude into the central pore of the unfoldase hexamer.
source: In general, this is accomplished by gripping the substrate polypeptide with aromatic side chains of loops (the highly-conserved pore-1 loops) that protrude into the central pore of the unfoldase hexamer.
evidence: This claim represents established scientific knowledge about AAA+ unfoldase mechanism.

claim: ATP hydrolysis drives conformational changes in the hexamer that pivot pore loops downward, applying mechanical force to the substrate.
source: ATP hydrolysis drives conformational changes in the hexamer that pivot these loops downward, thus applying a mechanical force from the site of engagement on the substrate, eventually unfolding it and translocating the unfolded polypeptide (Sauer and Baker, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to a review article (Sauer and Baker, 2011).

claim: The fundamental unfoldase-peptidase architecture and mechanism is used by eukaryotic and archaeal proteasomes and by several unfoldase-peptidase complexes shared among bacteria, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and chloroplasts.
source: This fundamental unfoldase-peptidase architecture and mechanism is used by eukaryotic and archaeal proteasomes and by several unfoldase-peptidase complexes shared among bacteria, mitochondria, peroxisomes, and chloroplasts (Sauer and Baker, 2011; Saibil, 2013; Quirós et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to review articles (Sauer and Baker, 2011; Saibil, 2013; Quirós et al., 2015).

claim: Bacterial ClpX with its partner peptidase ClpP is particularly specialized for regulatory degradation of substrates rather than for protein quality control.
source: One such bacterial unfoldase, ClpX, with its partner peptidase ClpP, is particularly specialized for regulatory degradation of substrates rather than for protein quality control, conditionally selecting a varied repertoire of substrates to execute stress responses and cell fate decisions (Gottesman, 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gottesman, 2003.

claim: Mitochondrial ClpX similarly acts in a regulatory capacity.
source: Accumulating evidence indicates that mitochondrial ClpX (mtClpX) similarly acts in a regulatory capacity, although only a few substrates of mtClpX have been verified and the regulatory consequences of its actions on mitochondrial physiology are largely undetermined (Kardon et al., 2015; Szczepanowska et al., 2016; Haynes et al., 2010; Matsushima et al., 2017; Kasashima et al., 2012; Al-Furoukh et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies (Kardon et al., 2015; Szczepanowska et al., 2016; Haynes et al., 2010; Matsushima et al., 2017; Kasashima et al., 2012; Al-Furoukh et al., 2014).

claim: The sequence preferences of mtClpX for substrate recognition diverge from those of bacterial ClpX.
source: How mtClpX recognizes its substrates also has not been characterized, although its sequence preferences for substrate recognition clearly diverge from those of bacterial ClpX (Martin et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Martin et al., 2008.

claim: ALAS treated with hydroxylamine followed by gel filtration remained slightly more than half-occupied with a species consistent with PLP-oxime.
source: We determined that ALAS treated with hydroxylamine followed by gel filtration remained slightly more than half-occupied with a species consistent with PLP-oxime (Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by fluorescence measurement data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2A,B.

claim: The activation of hydroxylamine-treated ALAS by mtClpX represents a combination of PLP binding to unoccupied active sites and exchange of PLP-oxime for PLP.
source: The activation of hydroxylamine-treated ALAS by mtClpX therefore represents a combination of PLP binding to unoccupied active sites and exchange of PLP-oxime for PLP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the PLP-oxime occupancy measurement.

claim: Both PLP binding to unoccupied active sites and exchange of PLP-oxime for PLP are likely useful in supporting ALAS function in vivo.
source: Both events are likely useful in supporting ALAS function in vivo, assisting de novo PLP binding and regenerating ALAS enzyme inactive due to a damaged cofactor (for example, PMP resulting from decarboxylation-coupled transamination of PLP, or other natural errors in catalysis [John, 1995]).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning supported by citation to John, 1995.

claim: Most residues sensitive to mutation in the mtClpX-binding peptides were perturbed by both alanine and aspartate substitutions.
source: In this array, we identified substitutions in each peptide that caused near-complete loss of mtClpX binding, with the exception of the most C-terminal peptide. Most residues sensitive to mutation were perturbed by both alanine and aspartate.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide array scanning data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: Several bulky hydrophobic amino acids (leucine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine) were highly represented in positions important for mtClpX interaction.
source: Several bulky hydrophobic amino acids (leucine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine) were highly represented in positions important for mtClpX interaction.
evidence: This claim is supported by peptide array scanning data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mtClpX-preferred residues (leucine, phenylalanine, and tyrosine) differ from the characterized preference of E. coli ClpX, for which alanine and basic residues are often important in substrate recognition.
source: This side-chain preference differed from the characterized preference of E. coli ClpX, for which alanine and basic residues are often important in substrate recognition (Flynn et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by comparison with cited literature (Flynn et al., 2003).

claim: The mtClpX-preferred residues comprise the set of signal residues observed to direct mitochondrial N-end rule-based degradation.
source: The mtClpX-preferred residues we observe are also notable in that they comprise the set of signal residues observed to direct mitochondrial N-end rule-based degradation (Vögtle et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Vögtle et al., 2009.

claim: Removing contacts between the protomers through F71A/Y73A mutations likely increases the solvent accessibility of the active site.
source: Removing contacts between the protomers through these mutations likely increases the solvent accessibility of the active site, thereby increasing the spontaneous PLP-ALAS binding rate at the expense of active site function.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on structural analysis and activity data.

claim: The reduced activity of ALASF71A/Y73A illustrates a potential cost of a more solvent-accessible active site and suggests an advantage of transient, unfoldase-induced accessibility.
source: The reduced activity of ALASF71A/Y73A therefore illustrates a potential cost of a more solvent-accessible active site and suggests an advantage of transient, unfoldase-induced accessibility.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the activity data for ALASF71A/Y73A.

claim: The rate of unfolding of protein substrates by ClpX homologs is often proportional to the local mechanical stability of the substrate protein at the site of initiation of unfolding.
source: Because the rate of unfolding of protein substrates by ClpX homologs is often proportional to the local mechanical stability of the substrate protein at the site of initiation of unfolding, this reduced contact may be responsible for the increased Vmax of mtClpX action on ALASF71A/Y73A.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about ClpX unfoldase mechanism.

claim: Residues F71 and Y73 in α1 participate both in mtClpX recognition and in forming stabilizing contacts across the dimer interface that suppress spontaneous PLP exchange and support ALAS activity.
source: These residues in α1 thus participate both in mtClpX recognition and in forming stabilizing contacts across the dimer interface that suppress spontaneous PLP exchange and support ALAS activity.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the combined mutagenesis, binding, kinetic, and activity data.

claim: The interaction of mtClpX with Y274 and possibly other residues in this peptide cluster promote rapid processing of ALAS.
source: This finding demonstrates the importance of contacts with ALAS outside of α1 for mtClpX action and suggests that the interaction of mtClpX with Y274 and possibly other residues in this peptide cluster promote rapid processing of ALAS.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the Y274A mutation data showing reduced Vmax.

claim: The compound mtClpX-binding site spanned by mutations F71, Y73, and Y274 is the physiological site at which mtClpX recognizes and begins acting on ALAS to promote ALAS activation and heme biosynthesis.
source: The concordance between the effect of mutations in ALAS on its activation by mtClpX in vitro and mtClpX-dependent ALA production in vivo support the compound mtClpX-binding site spanned by these mutations as the physiological site at which mtClpX recognizes and begins acting on ALAS to promote ALAS activation and thus heme biosynthesis.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the concordance between in vitro and in vivo data.

claim: Direct unfolding of some or all of α1 and β1–3 could increase solvent exposure of the active site and might also increase the conformational dynamics of active site-proximal elements.
source: Direct unfolding of some or all of α1 and β1–3 could increase solvent exposure of the active site and might also increase the conformational dynamics of active site-proximal elements that are contacted or indirectly stabilized by α1 and β1–3.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the hydrogen-deuterium exchange data.

claim: Unfolding enacted by mtClpX along the path from the N-terminus through α1 to the following β sheet could expose the active site and gate access for PLP.
source: Unfolding enacted by mtClpX along this short path could thus expose the active site and gate access for PLP.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the hydrogen-deuterium exchange and structural data.

claim: Several groups have recently observed mtClpX-dependent ALAS turnover under heme-replete conditions in vivo, directed by a heme-binding motif in ALAS.
source: Several groups have recently observed mtClpX-dependent ALAS turnover under heme-replete conditions in vivo, directed by a heme-binding motif in ALAS (Yien et al., 2017; Kubota et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Yien et al., 2017 and Kubota et al., 2016.

claim: The block to complete unfolding by mtClpX may be conditionally released in a feedback mechanism, allowing complete unfolding and degradation with mtClpP.
source: These observations suggest that the block to complete unfolding by mtClpX may be conditionally released in a feedback mechanism, allowing complete unfolding and degradation (with mtClpP).
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on cited observations of heme-dependent ALAS degradation.

claim: The heme-binding motif falls within the flexible N-terminal extension that serves as a sequence-independent grip site for mtClpX.
source: The heme-binding motif falls within the flexible N-terminal extension (which diverges widely in sequence, even among vertebrates) that we here propose as a sequence-independent grip site for mtClpX.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the location of the heme-binding motif and the characterization of the N-terminal extension.

claim: The N-terminal region of ALAS might serve as a bifunctional communication module for mtClpX, directing partial unfolding and activation when heme concentration is low, or ALAS degradation when heme concentration is high.
source: The N-terminal region of ALAS thus might serve as a bifunctional communication module for mtClpX, directing partial unfolding and activation when heme concentration is low, or ALAS degradation when heme concentration is high.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the heme-dependent degradation observations and the N-terminal extension characterization.

claim: Heme binding within the N-terminal initiating site could reconfigure ALAS interaction with mtClpX such that it begins unfolding from a different site with a lower barrier to unfolding, or could stabilize interaction with mtClpX to disfavor release.
source: Heme binding within this initiating site could reconfigure ALAS interaction with mtClpX such that it begins unfolding from a different site with a lower barrier to unfolding, or could stabilize interaction with mtClpX to disfavor release.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning about the mechanism of heme-dependent degradation.

claim: Some AAA+ unfoldases are dedicated modulators of one client protein.
source: Unlike ClpX, the proteasomal unfoldases, and other AAA+ unfoldases that act on a wide variety of substrates (such as E. coli ClpX, p97/Cdc48, ClpA, and ClpB/Hsp104), some AAA+ unfoldases are dedicated modulators of one client protein.
evidence: This claim represents established knowledge about AAA+ unfoldase diversity.

claim: Rca, which de-inhibits Rubisco, and Trip13, which inactivates the mitotic checkpoint by remodeling Mad2, carry out targeted unfolding of their client that does not appear to follow the stalling sequence/stable domain formula.
source: Several of these specialists, such as Rca, which de-inhibits Rubisco, or Trip13, which inactivates the mitotic checkpoint by remodeling Mad2, carry out targeted unfolding of their client that, like mtClpX with ALAS, does not appear to follow the stalling sequence/stable domain formula (Ye et al., 2015; Bhat et al., 2017; Brulotte et al., 2017; Alfieri et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Ye et al., 2015; Bhat et al., 2017; Brulotte et al., 2017; Alfieri et al., 2018.

claim: It has been proposed that Rca's maximum unfolding force is low and thus calibrated to allow unfolding of only the C-terminal b strand of Rubisco.
source: In the case of Rca, it has been proposed that its maximum unfolding force is low and thus calibrated to allow unfolding of only the C-terminal b strand of a Rubisco.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on Rca.

claim: Remodeling of MAD2 by TRIP13 destabilizes the ternary complex between TRIP13, MAD2, and their adaptor protein p31-comet, which may promote release of MAD2 by favoring TRIP13 hexamer disassembly.
source: In the case of TRIP13, remodeling of MAD2 destabilizes the ternary complex between TRIP13, MAD2, and their adaptor protein p31-comet, which may promote release of MAD2 by favoring TRIP13 hexamer disassembly.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to previous work on TRIP13.

claim: Substrate features and their interactions with the unfoldase may direct both specialist AAA+ unfoldases and generalist AAA+ unfoldases with specialized substrates.
source: Other substrate features and their interactions with the unfoldase may similarly direct both specialist AAA+ unfoldases and generalist AAA+ unfoldases with specialized substrates.
evidence: This claim is speculative reasoning based on the observations in this study and cited work.
